titolo: What Did Ordinary Families Actually Do With One Dollar During the Great Depression?
descrizione: How ordinary American families stretched one dollar during the Great Depression: the 1933 bank holiday, flour sack dresses, Dish Night at the movies, Pie Town, New Mexico, the CCC thirty-dollar paycheck, the first minimum wage and the three-cent stamp. Real 1930s history, prices and photographs, including Russell Lee's FSA work in the Library of Congress.

scene.testo: In March 1933, every bank in America closed its doors.
Overnight, a dollar in your hand beat a dollar in savings.
Today I'll show you where one dollar really went.
From a flour sack dress to a ten-cent movie.
But the strangest story is the one about dishes.
If your grandmother ever hid cash in a coffee can,
she probably learned it in those years.
Franklin Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933.
Two days later, he ordered a national bank holiday.
Thousands of banks had already failed by then.
Families lost their savings, and nobody paid them back.
Some towns printed their own paper scrip.
Merchants accepted it when real cash ran out.
Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act on March 9.
On March 12, Roosevelt spoke to the nation by radio.
He told people their money was safer in banks.
Families gathered around the radio to hear that fireside chat.
Banks reopened in stages over the following days.
Later that year, Congress created federal deposit insurance.
At first, it protected accounts up to twenty-five hundred dollars.
Still, trust came slowly, and wages came slower.
Now look closely at an ordinary cloth sack.
Flour, sugar, and animal feed often came in cotton bags.
Thrifty women washed them, bleached them, and sewed them.
Dish towels, pillowcases, aprons, and children's dresses came from them.
Then the bag makers noticed what women were doing.
Companies began printing bags with flowers, stripes, and plaid.
A mother might choose her feed by the pattern.
Companies even published booklets showing how to use the bags.
A dress needed more cloth than one bag held.
So mothers asked neighbors for matching sacks.
One purchase did two jobs: first feeding, then clothing.
No one called it fashion. It was just good sense.
Some quilts from those years still hold feed sack prints.
If your mother ever made a dress from scraps,
you are standing in the shadow of those sacks.
Now to the theater, and the story I promised.
Tens of millions of Americans still went to the movies each week.
Many matinee tickets cost about a dime.
Slow weeknights were when theaters needed crowds most.
So they got creative. One trick was called Dish Night.
Buy a ticket, and you received a piece of dinnerware.
One week a plate, the next week a cup.
Slowly, a family built a whole set.
The dishes were thin, cheap, and often brightly colored.
Another trick was Bank Night, a cash drawing.
Your ticket gave you a chance at the jackpot.
Inside, the movie offered two hours away from worry.
Cartoons, newsreels, and a feature, all for a few coins.
Those cheap dishes now sell in antique shops.
Collectors call them Depression glass.
A small dime bought a very long memory.
Now travel west, to a town named for dessert.
Pie Town, New Mexico, sits along U.S. Highway 60.
A man named Clyde Norman once sold pies there.
Travelers stopped, ate, and the name stuck.
In 1940, photographer Russell Lee arrived with his camera.
He worked for the Farm Security Administration.
His photographs are now in the Library of Congress.
He photographed homesteaders, their cabins, and their dinners.
Many had left the drought-struck plains.
They built their own cabins and dugout homes.
They grew pinto beans on dry land.
Water was hard to find, so every drop mattered.
Neighbors gathered for dances and community dinners.
Little cash changed hands in that high country.
People traded work, shared tools, and helped with harvests.
A dollar was only part of their wealth.
The rest was land, labor, and neighbors.
If you ever baked a pie for a neighbor,
you kept that old kind of money alive.
Now meet a paycheck that mostly never got spent.
In 1933, the Civilian Conservation Corps began.
It put young unemployed men to work outdoors.
They planted trees, fought fires, and built park trails.
The camps were organized like small towns of barracks.
They earned thirty dollars a month.
Twenty-five of those dollars went straight home.
They kept five dollars for themselves.
Housing, meals, and work clothes came with the job.
Back home, that check could pay the grocer.
Or the landlord, or the doctor.
About three million men served before the program ended in 1942.
Some learned to read in camp classes.
They built trails, bridges, and shelters in national parks.
Many of those structures are still standing.
Next time you hike a park trail, remember that paycheck.
Next, the price of one hour of work.
Before 1938, there was no national floor for wages.
In June 1938, Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act.
It set the first national minimum wage.
Twenty-five cents an hour.
Four hours of that work earned one dollar.
A full forty-four-hour week paid eleven dollars.
The law also limited the standard work week.
But many workers were left out at first.
Farm laborers and domestic workers were not covered.
For them, a dollar still came slowly.
A dime was about twenty-four minutes of minimum wage work.
Think about that at the checkout counter.
Now a smaller slice of the dollar: the mail.
In July 1932, a first-class stamp rose to three cents.
A postcard cost just one cent.
Thirty-three stamps cost ninety-nine cents.
For families split apart, letters were everything.
A son in a CCC camp wrote home.
A father looking for work wrote home.
Thousands of ordinary Americans wrote to the Roosevelts.
Some asked for help with rent or a winter coat.
Eleanor Roosevelt received a great many of those letters.
Those letters now fill archives.
Ordinary handwriting, keeping ordinary lives in ink.
The mail carrier was a welcome face on the street.
A postcard saying we are fine cost one cent.
Now the smallest coin, and a famous candy bar.
A Hershey bar cost five cents through those years.
A bottle of Coca-Cola cost a nickel too.
That soda price stayed put for decades.
Twenty nickels made one dollar.
The company kept the nickel price by changing the bar's size.
Milton Hershey kept building in Pennsylvania during the Depression.
In 1933, he began a grand hotel on the hill.
The project kept local workers employed.
He also built a community building and a stadium.
A nickel could buy a small, shared joy.
If your grandfather remembered a nickel soda,
he was remembering a price that never moved.
So what did one dollar really do?
It fed a family, one careful purchase at a time.
It turned a flour bag into a dress.
It bought an evening of light in a theater.
It crossed the country in a young man's envelope.
In Pie Town, it was shared along with the work.
After the bank failures, every saved dollar felt precious.
Radio brought one shared voice into millions of kitchens.
Families did not feel clever. They felt responsible.
Many kept string, jars, and saved sacks for decades.
If you remember a grandparent who wasted nothing,
now you know where that lesson came from.
One dollar, one table, and a family that held together.
